title: Read a Work Order Like a Mechanism Map
mechanism_check: A work order is a mechanism spec: location, asset, symptom, requested action. The mechanism is what the asset is supposed to do when healthy.
Most failed jobs start at intake, not in the field: the symptom described is not the mechanism that failed.
Your job before touching tools: restate the requested action as a mechanism statement - 'this valve should shut off flow to lot 4; it doesn't.'
improvised_tools: A blank work order form or notebook - rewrite the request in mechanism language before starting.
A phone camera: photograph the asset's nameplate and the symptom before you touch anything.
Whatever basic testers your trade carries - the kit extends your senses, not your judgment.
steps: Read the request twice; circle the asset, the symptom, and the requested action.
Restate as one mechanism sentence: what should happen versus what actually happens.
Ask the requester one clarifying question if the mechanism is ambiguous - cheap now, expensive later.
Check the asset history: prior work orders on the same asset name the pattern.
Confirm you have the right location and the right asset before loading tools.
Write your mechanism sentence on the work order so the next crew inherits it.
stop_conditions: Stop if the asset's identity is ambiguous and nobody can confirm - working on the wrong valve shuts off the wrong block.
Stop if the request asks for work outside your crew's authorization or a licensed trade's scope.
Stop if the requested action would bypass a safety device - escalate to a supervisor.

title: Improvise Temporary Traffic Control for a Small Road Job
mechanism_check: Drivers need three things: warning before the work zone, guidance through it, and a clear end. Without all three, the zone fails.
Traffic control is a mechanism of expectations: every device tells a driver what to do next, in sequence.
The taper is the critical mechanism: it shifts traffic smoothly instead of slamming it into a wall of cones.
improvised_tools: Cones, barrels, or anything tall and visible that marks a line - borrow across depots if short.
Advance-warning signs; when signs are short, a second spotter with a flag acts as the warning device.
High-visibility vests for every person outside a vehicle - non-negotiable.
A vehicle with flashers parked upstream as a shadow vehicle when a crash truck is unavailable.
steps: Read your jurisdiction's temporary traffic control manual for the minimum layout for your road speed.
Place advance warning first, working back from the work area toward traffic - last device placed first.
Set the taper by shifting one lane width over the required taper length; never shorter.
Assign one person as spotter; their only job is traffic, not the work.
Walk the approach as a driver would: if any device is confusing from a car seat, fix it.
Pull the zone in reverse order at the end of the shift - never leave orphaned devices.
stop_conditions: Stop if you cannot field the minimum device layout for the road's posted speed - an under-signed zone is a liability, not a workaround.
Stop and escalate to the engineer if the road is high-speed or high-volume and you only have hand flags.
Stop if a driver-facing device fails at night: close the zone until retroreflectivity or lighting is restored.
Never improvise with your own body as the barrier - no device substitutes for a human life.

title: Patch a Pothole That Holds
mechanism_check: A pothole fails from its edges, not its center: water gets under the patch edge and pops it loose.
The mechanism of a lasting patch is edge bond plus compaction plus drainage - throw-and-go skips all three.
Cold mix works by compaction, not chemistry: density is the patch's strength.
improvised_tools: A tamper or any flat heavy steel for compaction when the plate compactor is elsewhere.
A wire brush or stiff broom to clean the hole's edges - bond needs clean asphalt.
The jurisdiction-approved tack; when none is available, a clean dry edge beats a dirty oiled one.
A straightedge or shovel blade to check the patch sits slightly proud, not low.
steps: Clear water, loose material, and debris from the hole - bond needs a clean, firm edge.
Square the edges where you can; sound edges hold better than crumbly rims.
Fill in thin lifts, tamping each lift hard - compaction in layers, not one loose dump.
Crown the patch slightly above grade; traffic will settle it flush, not hollow.
Seal the edge seam if you have tack; a sealed edge keeps water out of the bond.
Log the location, material used, and conditions on the work order for the next crew.
stop_conditions: Stop if standing water fills the hole and no drain is possible - patching a pond wastes material.
Stop if the failure is a base failure (pumping, alligator cracking around it) - it needs a dig-out, not a patch; escalate.
Stop if the patch sits over a utility cut or sinkhole - the mechanism below is unknown; investigate first.

title: Diagnose a Blocked Storm Drain
mechanism_check: Storm flow is gravity's work: water falls to the lowest open path. A backup means the path is blocked, undersized, or submerged.
Diagnose downstream-first: if downstream is blocked, clearing upstream does nothing.
The grate is the first filter: most 'blocked drains' are blocked grates, not blocked pipes.
improvised_tools: A rake and shovel - clear the grate before assuming a pipe problem.
A jug of water to test flow direction and locate the stall point.
A flashlight and mirror to look down the pipe without entering.
A probe rod or stiff wire to feel for soft blockages within arm's reach.
steps: Check the grate first: clear leaves, trash, and sediment from the inlet.
Look downstream: is the outfall submerged or blocked? A submerged outfall is a tailwater problem, not a pipe problem.
Test with water: pour upstream and watch where it stalls - the stall point is the blockage.
Probe soft blockages within reach; hard obstructions need the jetter or vactor truck.
Check the catch basin sump: a full sump is normal; sediment above the pipe invert is not.
Report the blockage location, type, and upstream/downstream conditions for the cleaning crew.
stop_conditions: Never enter a manhole or confined space without the full confined-space program: tripod, air monitor, attendant, rescue plan.
Stop if water is backing into buildings or a roadway is flooding - escalate to emergency response; beyond routine clearing.
Stop if the blockage is a collapsed pipe or an object you cannot identify - call engineering before disturbing it.
Stop if the flow smells of chemicals or shows a sewage cross-connection - that is a hazmat and environmental call, not a shovel job.

title: Stand Up a Temporary Public Service Counter
mechanism_check: A service counter is a mechanism for two flows: people who need answers, and documents that need intake. It fails when the flows tangle.
Trust is the mechanism underneath: citizens need to see order, signage, and a person who owns their case.
The counter's real product is not the transaction - it is the citizen's confidence the transaction happened.
improvised_tools: Folding tables and chairs from any city facility - a counter is furniture plus process.
Printed signage from any office printer: big letters, one message per sign, arrows where needed.
A numbered ticket system: sticky notes or torn paper work when the take-a-number machine does not.
A lockable box or cabinet for documents - chain of custody starts at intake.
steps: Pick the site: accessible, covered, visible from the approach, with parking.
Split the flows: one line for questions, one intake point for documents - never both at one table.
Post three signs minimum: what this counter does, what to bring, where the line forms.
Give every citizen a receipt for every document taken: name, date, what was received, who took it.
Keep a simple log: sequence number, name, need, outcome - this is your audit trail.
Brief every volunteer and staffer on the one thing this counter cannot do, so they all say it the same way.
stop_conditions: Stop taking originals if you cannot secure them - tell citizens to bring copies until storage is locked.
Stop if the site becomes unsafe (weather, crowd size, threats) - move or close, never tough it out.
Stop and escalate any request outside the counter's authority - improvising approvals is malfeasance, not improvisation.
Stop if records handling would violate your jurisdiction's retention or privacy rules - ask before inventing a system.

title: Triage a Permit Intake Queue
mechanism_check: A permit queue is a flow mechanism: applications enter, review consumes staff-hours, decisions exit. Backlog is input exceeding throughput.
Not all applications cost the same: simple over-the-counter permits and complex plan reviews are different species in one queue.
Triage's mechanism is sorting by completeness and complexity, not by arrival order.
improvised_tools: A one-page completeness checklist per permit type - the single highest-leverage tool in permitting.
Colored folders or labels: green complete, yellow needs info, red complex review.
A shared log: date in, checklist status, reviewer assigned, date out.
Standard deficiency letters: pre-written, specific, checkable - so applicants fix it in one round.
steps: Sort the intake pile by permit type first, then check each against the completeness checklist.
Complete simple applications go straight to approval or the short queue - do not let them drown behind complex ones.
Incomplete applications get one specific deficiency letter listing exactly what is missing.
Complex applications get an assigned reviewer and a target date - uncertainty is what generates angry phone calls.
Publish the current average turnaround per permit type where applicants can see it.
Re-triage weekly: queues drift; triage is a rhythm, not an event.
stop_conditions: Stop if the backlog is hiding safety reviews (structural, fire, electrical) behind cosmetic permits - life-safety reviews never wait for convenience.
Stop 'expediting' that is actually skipping review steps - that is negligence with paperwork, not triage.
Stop if the completeness checklist is being applied unevenly across applicants - inconsistent standards are a fairness and legal problem; escalate.

title: Walk a Permit From Application to Sign-Off
mechanism_check: A permit is a chain of verifications: each review confirms one mechanism - structure holds, wiring is safe, egress works.
The applicant's enemy is ambiguity; the reviewer's enemy is rework. The mechanism that serves both is specific, checkable feedback.
Sign-off is not approval of the building - it is the record that the required verifications happened.
improvised_tools: A status board or spreadsheet: every application, every review stage, current owner, days at stage.
A correction template with numbered items, code sections cited, and a re-review checklist.
A phone log: one call now prevents three review cycles later.
Sample approved plans as examples - show applicants what 'right' looks like.
steps: Confirm intake completeness against the checklist before any reviewer touches the application.
Route to reviewers in dependency order: site before structure, structure before systems - do not parallelize what sequences.
Write corrections as numbered, citable, checkable items - vague comments breed resubmits.
Offer a pre-submittal meeting for complex projects: an hour of guidance saves weeks of cycles.
Track days-per-stage; when one stage balloons, that is where the process is broken.
At sign-off, file the complete record: application, plans, reviews, corrections, approvals - the record is the product.
stop_conditions: Stop if pressure - political, financial, or social - asks you to skip a required review or sign off unverified work. Document the pressure and escalate.
Stop if the applicant's plans conceal the real scope - send it back for truthful plans.
Stop if you are asked to inspect or approve work in a trade you are not qualified to judge - request a qualified reviewer.
Never backdate or pre-sign anything. The date on the record is the date the verification happened.

title: Run a Field Inspection Without the Lab
mechanism_check: Inspection is mechanism verification in the field: does this installation match the mechanism the code requires?
Field tests answer binary questions: bonded or not, level or not, covered or not. You do not need a lab for binary.
Your eyes are the primary instrument; improvised tools extend them - they do not replace judgment.
improvised_tools: A camera: photo evidence beats memory in every dispute and every report.
The field kit's core four: tape, level, multimeter, moisture meter.
A mirror and flashlight for seeing behind, above, and inside without demolition.
Reference cards: the code sections you enforce most, condensed to pocket size.
steps: Review the permit and plans before you arrive - know what you are verifying before you see it.
Start with life-safety items: egress, structural, fire separation, grounding.
Test, do not eyeball, the critical five: bonding, clearances, cover depths, fastening schedules, labeling.
Photograph every deficiency with a reference object for scale.
Explain deficiencies on site in mechanism language: what fails, why it matters, what passes.
Write the report the same day: delay is where details die.
stop_conditions: Stop if the site is unsafe to enter - no inspection is worth an injury; reschedule and document.
Stop if you are asked to pass work you did not verify - 'it was fine last time' is not an inspection.
Stop if the contractor pressures, threatens, or offers inducements: leave, document, report.
Stop and call the lab or specialist for anything your field tools cannot answer - knowing the edge of your kit is the skill.

title: Patch Public Infrastructure on a Thin Budget
mechanism_check: A thin budget is a prioritization mechanism, not permission to do bad work: it forces the question 'what fails next?'
Deferred maintenance compounds: a small seal today is a rebuild in five years. The budget's enemy is the deferral curve.
The mechanism of cheap-but-right: extend asset life at the cheapest intervention point that still works.
improvised_tools: A prioritized asset list: condition, consequence of failure, cost of intervention - sorted by risk, not complaint volume.
Crack seal, patch mix, paint, and grease: the four cheapest life-extenders in public works.
Borrowed equipment from neighboring jurisdictions - mutual aid applies to graders too.
Volunteer and community-service labor for low-skill prep work under crew supervision.
steps: Rank every candidate job by consequence times likelihood of failure - fix what fails worst first.
Spend the first dollars on preventive work (sealing, painting, greasing) that stops the deferral curve.
Break big repairs into phased interventions the budget can absorb year by year.
Document every deferral: what was postponed, the risk accepted, who accepted it - in writing.
Track unit costs so next year's budget request carries real numbers, not guesses.
Close the loop with the public: show what the budget fixed - visibility protects next year's budget.
stop_conditions: Stop if a deferral puts life safety at risk - no budget constraint overrides a known safety hazard; escalate in writing.
Stop if 'cheap' means unlicensed work, substandard materials on a regulated asset, or skipping required inspections.
Stop spending when the appropriation is exhausted - overspending an appropriation is unlawful in most jurisdictions; get an amendment first.
Stop if the repair would violate grant or funding-source restrictions - know what the money is allowed to buy.

title: Run a Neighborhood Cleanup With Volunteers
mechanism_check: Volunteers are a surge mechanism: high energy, low training, short attention. The mechanism that works is many small bounded tasks, not one big project.
Safety is the binding constraint: volunteers get hurt when nobody owns safety.
The real product is civic ownership - the cleanup is the excuse; the neighborhood taking the block back is the outcome.
improvised_tools: Borrowed trucks, trailers, and roll-offs from public works - the city's equipment is the community's equipment.
Donated bags, gloves, and water from local businesses - ask; civic pride is an easy sell.
A simple sign-in sheet: name, contact, emergency contact - your accountability record.
A printed zone map with team assignments - one page, readable at arm's length.
steps: Walk the area first: scope the work, spot hazards (needles, chemicals, unstable structures), set the boundary.
Divide the area into zones small enough that a team can finish one in the time you have.
Brief every volunteer on safety first, then the task: gloves, closed shoes, what not to touch, where the first-aid kit is.
Assign team leads - one accountable adult per zone, with check-ins on a schedule.
Stage collection points so volunteers carry short distances and trucks haul long ones.
End with visible results and thanks: before/after photos, a count of bags, public credit - volunteers return when the work mattered.
stop_conditions: Stop any volunteer from handling hazardous materials - needles, chemicals, asbestos suspect: that is a trained crew's job.
Stop work in any zone that becomes unsafe: traffic intrusion, unstable structures, severe weather.
Stop if minors are present without proper supervision ratios - know your jurisdiction's volunteer rules.
Stop if the collected material includes evidence of illegal dumping that needs investigation - report before hauling it away.

title: Improvise Ice and Snow Response When the Plow Is Down
mechanism_check: Snow response is a priority mechanism: arterials, then collectors, then residential - the network fails at the arterials first.
Traction is friction's work: salt lowers the freezing point, sand adds grip, plowing removes mass. Each is a different mechanism - use the right one.
The improvisation principle: partial service on the right streets beats full service attempted everywhere.
improvised_tools: Any truck with a blade or bucket: loaders, graders, even backhoes clear in a pinch.
Hand spreaders, shovels, and push brooms for walks, steps, and hydrants - the parts plows cannot reach anyway.
Sand and salt mix applied by hand at intersections, hills, and curves - the highest-value handfuls.
Volunteer 4x4s or contractor trucks under a simple call-list - know your surge capacity before the storm.
steps: Declare the priority map: arterials and emergency routes first, posted where crews and the public can see it.
Reassign every available vehicle by capability, not by title - a loader is a plow today.
Hit the critical points by hand: intersections, hills, hospital and fire-station approaches, hydrants.
Communicate the plan publicly: which streets, in what order, when to expect service - silence breeds 911 calls.
Rotate crews: fatigue in a storm kills as surely as ice does.
After the storm, log what worked and what was missing - the after-action is next storm's equipment list.
stop_conditions: Stop operations when conditions make the response itself unsafe - whiteout, ice under equipment, crew exhaustion; a crashed plow helps nobody.
Stop if a makeshift vehicle or attachment is unsafe for road use - an improvised blade that fails on a highway is a weapon.
Stop applying salt near waterways beyond your jurisdiction's environmental limits - know the runoff rules.
Never clear snow onto a traveled lane or block a hydrant, crosswalk, or accessible ramp.

title: De-Escalate a Service-Counter Confrontation
mechanism_check: Escalation is a threat-response mechanism: the citizen feels unheard, powerless, or wronged, and volume is their last tool.
De-escalation's mechanism is restoring the person's sense of agency: heard, options, control over something.
Your calm is contagious in both directions - the mechanism works through you first.
improvised_tools: A private or semi-private space to move the conversation out of the public queue - audience fuels escalation.
A supervisor on call - knowing backup exists keeps you calm, which keeps them calm.
Plain-language explanations: most anger at counters is confusion wearing a loud voice.
A notepad: writing down their concern proves it is being taken seriously.
steps: Let them finish the first wave without interrupting - the venting has a bottom.
Name what you heard: 'So the permit was denied and nobody explained why.' Being heard lowers the temperature.
Separate the person from the problem: 'Let's fix the application' - you and them against the paperwork.
Offer real options, not sympathy: two paths forward the citizen can choose between.
Set the boundary calmly if it crosses: 'I want to help you, and I need us to keep this respectful.'
Document the incident factually afterward: what happened, what was said, what was decided.
stop_conditions: Stop the conversation and get help if there are threats of violence, weapons, or you feel unsafe - no service interaction is worth injury.
Stop if the person is impaired, in crisis, or a danger to themselves - this is a public-safety call, not a service call.
Stop defending a decision you do not understand - say so honestly and get the person who can explain it.
Never make promises outside your authority to defuse the moment - a false promise becomes tomorrow's bigger confrontation.

title: Document Field Work So It Survives an Audit
mechanism_check: An audit tests one mechanism: can a stranger reconstruct what happened, when, by whom, and why - from the record alone?
Memory is not a record. If it is not written, photographed, and dated, it did not happen - that is the auditor's rule.
The record's real audience is future-you under oath. Write for that person.
improvised_tools: A bound notebook or numbered form: sequential, dated, no torn pages - the cheapest audit-proofing there is.
A phone camera with timestamps on: before, during, after - photos are the record's spine.
A simple daily log template: date, crew, weather, work performed, materials used, hours, anomalies.
Copies kept in two places - truck and office, or phone and server.
steps: Log the work daily, same format every day - consistency is what makes records credible.
Record the four anchors on every entry: who, what, where, when. Add why when the work deviates from plan.
Photograph before, during, and after - and photograph the anomalies, not just the successes.
Note materials by quantity and source: the auditor's favorite question is 'where did it go?'
Have a supervisor or peer sign off weekly - a witnessed record beats an unwitnessed one.
File promptly: a record written a month later is a reconstruction, and auditors know the difference.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are asked to alter, backdate, or omit records - that is falsification, and it is the fastest career-ender in public service.
Stop using personal devices or accounts for official records if your jurisdiction's records policy requires official channels - follow the policy.
Stop if the documentation reveals a safety or legal problem - report it up; the record is evidence, not a confession to bury.
Never destroy records to 'clean up' - follow the retention schedule; premature destruction is its own violation.

title: Stretch a Fiscal-Year Budget Quarter to Quarter
mechanism_check: A fiscal year is a burn-rate mechanism: the budget must last twelve months, but spending pressure is never evenly distributed.
The two classic failures: running dry in Q4 (no reserves for emergencies) or panic-spending in Q4 (use-it-or-lose-it waste).
The mechanism that works: planned reserves, phased spending, and honest forecasting - cash flow, not just totals.
improvised_tools: A simple quarterly burn chart: planned versus actual, updated monthly - one page, no fancy software needed.
A prioritized deferral list: what can slip to next quarter, what cannot.
Bulk and cooperative purchasing: neighboring jurisdictions buying together get better prices.
Preventive maintenance spending: the cheapest dollars in any public-works budget.
steps: Divide the annual budget into quarterly targets with a reserve held for Q4 emergencies.
Track actual versus planned monthly - a two-month drift caught early is a correction; caught in Q4 it is a crisis.
Front-load preventive and high-ROI work; push discretionary projects to quarters with slack.
When a quarter runs hot, cut from the deferral list in priority order - never from reserves or safety work.
Use cooperative purchasing and bulk buys to stretch every procurement dollar.
Build next year's request on this year's real unit costs - honest numbers defend budgets better than stories.
stop_conditions: Stop before overspending the appropriation - in most jurisdictions that is unlawful; get an amendment or transfer approved first.
Stop end-of-year panic spending to 'protect' next year's budget - waste is waste, and auditors notice patterns.
Stop if spending would violate fund restrictions - restricted money buys restricted things, full stop.
Stop and escalate when a genuine emergency needs money that is not there - document the need, request emergency authorization, do not freelance the spending.

title: Coordinate Multi-Agency Incident Response
mechanism_check: Multi-agency response fails at the seams: unclear command, duplicated effort, incompatible radios, nobody owning the public message.
The mechanism that works is unified command with a single incident action plan - one plan, many agencies.
Coordination's currency is the common operating picture: everyone working from the same facts.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard or butcher paper with the incident objectives, org chart, and situation map - the common picture made visible.
A liaison from each agency with authority to commit their agency's resources - liaisons without authority are decoration.
A shared radio channel or phone bridge - interoperability you build in the first hour, not the third.
A written incident action plan, even one page: objectives, assignments, safety, communications.
steps: Establish unified command immediately: who commands what, documented and announced to all agencies.
Build the common operating picture: situation map, resources on scene, resources needed, public message.
Write the incident action plan for the next operational period - objectives first, tactics second.
Assign a liaison officer and a public information officer: seams and messaging are named jobs, not afterthoughts.
Hold briefings on a fixed cycle - rhythm replaces rumor.
Demobilize deliberately: release resources in order, document everything, schedule the after-action.
stop_conditions: Stop freelancing: any unit operating outside the incident action plan is a liability - bring them in or stand them down.
Stop if command is disputed - resolve the authority question immediately; two commanders is worse than none.
Stop if responder safety is compromised by the plan - no objective justifies predictable casualties; revise the plan.
Stop and escalate to the next jurisdiction level when the incident exceeds local capability - that is what mutual aid and emergency declarations are for.

title: Build a Redundant Emergency Communication Tree
mechanism_check: Emergency communication fails by single points: one phone system, one contact list, one person who knows the plan.
The mechanism is redundancy at every layer: multiple channels, multiple contact paths, multiple people who can activate.
A tree that only works on work phones during work hours is not a tree - it is a hope.
improvised_tools: A printed contact tree - laminated, in every vehicle and office - that works when the network does not.
Group text, radio nets, and a phone bridge as three independent channels; assume one will fail.
A check-in protocol: branches confirm up the tree on a schedule, so silence is itself a signal.
A designated alternate for every key role - depth, not just breadth.
steps: Map the people who must be reachable: leadership, crews, mutual-aid partners, key facilities.
Assign each person two contact paths (for example radio plus cell) and one alternate who can reach them.
Print and distribute the tree - digital is primary, paper is the backup that never needs charging.
Build the activation protocol: who can activate, the exact words, the confirmation requirement.
Exercise the tree quarterly: an untested tree is a rumor.
Update the tree whenever personnel change - a stale tree is worse than none, because it looks reliable.
stop_conditions: Stop relying on any single channel for life-safety messages - confirm critical messages across two channels.
Stop if the tree includes people who have not agreed to be on it and trained on the protocol - unwilling nodes break the tree.
Stop if personal contact information is being shared beyond the need-to-know circle - protect privacy even in emergencies.
Never activate the emergency tree for non-emergencies - every false alarm spends the credibility the next real one needs.

title: Run Emergency Procurement Inside the Rules
mechanism_check: Emergency procurement exists because disasters do not wait for bid cycles - but the emergency exception is narrow and audited.
The mechanism: document the emergency, use the minimum deviation necessary, compete what you can, record everything.
The auditor's future question is always: was it truly an emergency, and did you buy only what the emergency required?
improvised_tools: Your jurisdiction's emergency procurement policy, printed and in the go-bag - know the thresholds before the emergency.
A pre-qualified vendor list for likely emergencies: fuel, generators, contractors, debris haulers.
A simple emergency purchase log: date, item, vendor, amount, justification, authorizer.
Template justifications: pre-written emergency rationale language you fill in, not invent under pressure.
steps: Confirm the situation meets your jurisdiction's legal definition of emergency - not urgent, not important: emergency.
Get the authorizer's approval in writing (even an email) before spending - authority first, purchase second.
Buy only what the emergency requires: scope discipline is what survives the audit.
Compete where you can, even informally - two quotes by phone beats one vendor by habit.
Log every purchase the same day: what, from whom, how much, why this vendor, who authorized.
Close out with a full emergency procurement file: declaration, approvals, quotes, receipts, justification memo.
stop_conditions: Stop if it is not a genuine emergency - using emergency powers for convenience is procurement fraud.
Stop at your authorization limit: purchases above it need the higher authority's signature, emergency or not.
Stop if a vendor demands terms that waive your jurisdiction's standard protections - emergency does not mean unprotected.
Stop and escalate conflicts of interest immediately - buying from family or friends under emergency powers is how careers end.

title: Restore Public Services After a Facility Failure
mechanism_check: A failed facility breaks services in dependency order: the failure cascades downstream until something stops it.
Restoration's mechanism is triage by criticality: life-safety services first, then essential operations, then everything else.
The public does not need the facility back - they need the services back. The facility is a means.
improvised_tools: A service-dependency map: which services die when this facility dies - drawn before the failure, used during it.
Temporary sites: other city buildings, rented trailers, tents - service location is negotiable, service is not.
Manual workarounds: paper forms, cash boxes, phone trees - the analog fallback for digital services.
A public-facing status board: what is down, what is working, where to go instead.
steps: Secure the failed facility: safety first, then assess - nobody restores services from inside a hazard.
List every service the facility provided and rank by criticality: life-safety, essential, deferrable.
Stand up temporary service points for the critical tier immediately - even folding tables count.
Publish the status: what is down, workarounds, where to go - silence is the second disaster.
Restore in criticality order, testing each service before announcing it back.
Run the full after-action: what failed, what the workaround cost, what redundancy to build before the next failure.
stop_conditions: Stop if re-entering or reusing the facility is unsafe - a standing building is not a safe building until inspected.
Stop restoring non-critical services while critical ones are still down - sequence discipline.
Stop if the workaround would violate records, privacy, or cash-handling rules - improvise the location, not the controls.
Stop and declare for higher-level aid when local restoration exceeds local resources - that is what the declaration process exists for.

title: Turn Field Experience Into a Certification
mechanism_check: Certifications convert invisible skill into portable proof: the mechanism is third-party validation of what your hands already know.
In public-sector careers, pay grades and promotions run on documented credentials - experience without paper is a discount you give your employer.
The mechanism of getting certified: map experience to requirements, fill the gaps, document the hours, pass the test.
improvised_tools: Your jurisdiction's or union's credential map: which certs unlock which pay steps.
An hours log: dates, tasks, supervisors - the raw material of every application.
Free or cheap prep: library materials, study groups, agency training budgets, union education funds.
A mentor who is certified: the fastest map through any application process.
steps: List the certifications that matter in your trade and jurisdiction - water, wastewater, pesticide, CDL, inspection, emergency management.
Pick the one with the best pay-step-per-effort ratio and confirm the exact requirements.
Map your logged hours against the requirements - most field workers are closer than they think.
Fill gaps deliberately: the cheapest qualifying training first, employer-paid where possible.
Apply with complete documentation - incomplete applications are the top reason for delay.
Once certified, log the renewal requirements immediately - lapsed certs cost more than maintained ones.
stop_conditions: Stop if a 'certification' is a pay-to-print mill with no recognized body behind it - verify accreditation before spending.
Stop pursuing a cert that requires experience you do not have and cannot get - pick the reachable one first.
Stop if the employer promises reimbursement but will not put it in writing - get the commitment documented.
Never misrepresent hours or experience on an application - that is fraud, and certifying bodies revoke.

title: Keep a Personal Skills Ledger
mechanism_check: Careers advance on evidence, not memory: the ledger is the mechanism that turns daily work into a promotable record.
Supervisors write evaluations from what they remember; the ledger makes sure they remember correctly.
The ledger's mechanism is compounding: small entries, kept daily, become an undeniable record over years.
improvised_tools: A notebook or simple document: date, task, skill used, outcome - five lines a day.
Photos of completed work with dates - visual proof beats adjectives.
Copies of commendations, training certificates, and good evaluations - the evidence file.
A quarterly review ritual: fifteen minutes reading the quarter back, noting the pattern.
steps: Log daily: what you did, what skill it used, what the outcome was - terse, factual, dated.
Capture the hard ones: emergencies handled, problems solved, money saved, people helped.
File the evidence: certificates, commendations, completed projects, before-and-after photos.
Review quarterly: what skills grew, what is missing, what the next certification or assignment should be.
Bring the ledger to every evaluation and every promotion conversation - let the record speak.
Keep a copy outside work systems - your record is yours; agency systems are the agency's.
stop_conditions: Stop logging anything that would violate records or privacy policy - keep it to your work and your skills, not citizens' data.
Stop if the ledger becomes fiction - inflate nothing; one caught exaggeration poisons the whole record.
Stop sharing the ledger's contents beyond what is needed for the evaluation or application - it is a career tool, not a diary.
Never use agency time or systems against policy to maintain it - keep it clean and compliant.

title: Cross-Train Into a Neighboring Trade
mechanism_check: Cross-training is a versatility mechanism: every adjacent skill you hold makes you deployable, promotable, and layoff-resistant.
The mechanism of learning a neighboring trade: you already know the context (the job site, the assets, the crew) - you only need the trade's specific mechanisms.
In public works, the highest-value cross-training is whatever your crew is always short of.
improvised_tools: The crew's experts: a standing offer to shadow on slow days costs nothing and teaches everything.
Slow periods and standby time: dead time is training time if you claim it.
Agency training budgets and union apprenticeship funds - money already allocated for exactly this.
A personal skills ledger to track the new competencies as they accumulate.
steps: Pick the neighboring trade your crew most often waits on - that is the one with the highest return.
Ask the expert to narrate while they work: mechanism first, then technique - learn the why before the how.
Start with the trade's foundation tasks under supervision: the safe, bounded, repeatable work.
Log every supervised task in your ledger - documented practice is what qualifies you.
Earn the trade's entry credential if one exists - the paper makes the skill official.
Offer the skill back: volunteer for the jobs that used to wait on someone else.
stop_conditions: Stop at the licensed line: cross-training never authorizes unlicensed electrical, plumbing, or other regulated work - assist, do not freelance.
Stop if the 'training' is just being used as free labor without teaching - name it and renegotiate.
Stop if you are asked to sign off or certify work in the new trade before you are qualified - your signature is your liability.
Stop if the new trade's safety training has not happened yet - the mechanism of the trade includes its hazards.

title: Mentor a New Hire or Apprentice
mechanism_check: Mentoring is a force-multiplier mechanism: one competent mentor produces competent crew members for years.
The mechanism that works is narrated work: the mentor does the job while explaining the mechanism, then watches the apprentice do it.
New hires fail from ambiguity, not inability - the mentor's job is removing ambiguity faster than the job creates it.
improvised_tools: A first-week checklist: the thirty things every new hire needs to know, in order.
Narrated work: 'watch me, then do it with me, then do it while I watch' - the oldest teaching mechanism there is.
A standing ten-minute debrief: what went well, what to change, one thing to learn tomorrow.
Your own mistakes as teaching material - the mentor who admits errors teaches judgment, not just technique.
steps: Start with the mechanisms, not the tasks: why this crew does what it does, in what order.
Demonstrate, then hand over: watch once, do together, do supervised, do solo - in that order.
Give the apprentice real work early - bounded, supervised, consequential enough to matter.
Debrief daily for the first month: short, specific, one correction and one win.
Introduce them to the crew as a future peer, not a burden - belonging accelerates learning.
Sign off competencies in writing as they are earned - the record protects you both.
stop_conditions: Stop if the apprentice is being assigned work beyond their qualification - your signature on their training is your responsibility.
Stop if mentoring becomes hazing or busywork - that is not training, that is liability.
Stop if you are asked to sign off competencies the apprentice has not demonstrated - paper without proof helps nobody.
Stop and escalate if the new hire is unsafe despite coaching - some people need a different role, and naming it early is kinder.

title: Build a Portfolio That Proves Public Value
mechanism_check: A portfolio is a proof mechanism: it converts years of invisible public work into visible, checkable evidence.
In public-sector careers, the people who decide promotions rarely saw the work - the portfolio is how they see it.
The mechanism is outcomes, not activities: problems solved, money saved, services restored, citizens helped.
improvised_tools: Before-and-after photos of projects, with dates and locations - the portfolio's backbone.
Work-order summaries and project records: scope, your role, outcome, cost.
Commendations, thank-you letters, and evaluation excerpts - third-party proof.
A one-page summary per project: problem, action, result, your specific contribution.
steps: Inventory your best work: the projects where something measurable got better because of you.
For each, write the one-pager: problem, your action, measurable result.
Collect the evidence: photos, records, letters, data - attach it to the story.
Quantify everything you honestly can: dollars saved, days cut, complaints resolved, uptime improved.
Organize by the competencies your jurisdiction's promotion system rewards - speak its language.
Update it yearly: a portfolio is a living record, not a one-time project.
stop_conditions: Stop if the 'evidence' includes citizens' personal data - anonymize or exclude; privacy rules apply to portfolios too.
Stop claiming sole credit for team work - credit the crew; claiming otherwise is dishonest and discoverable.
Stop if building it requires misusing agency systems or time - keep it compliant.
Never fabricate metrics - one invented number destroys the credibility of every real one.

title: Run an After-Action on Your Own Shift
mechanism_check: An after-action is a learning mechanism: it converts experience into improvement before the experience fades.
The mechanism is blameless review: what happened, why, what to keep, what to change - the person is never the problem, the process is.
Crews that debrief get better; crews that do not repeat - that is the whole mechanism.
improvised_tools: Fifteen minutes and four questions: what was supposed to happen, what actually happened, why the difference, what to change.
The shift log and any photos - facts, not memories.
A shared improvement list: one owner per item, one date per item.
The crew's own honesty - which only exists if the review is truly blameless.
steps: Hold it soon - same day if possible; memory decays fast and stories harden.
Walk the timeline: what was supposed to happen versus what actually happened, step by step.
Ask why repeatedly on the surprises - the mechanism behind the deviation is the lesson.
Separate luck from skill: what worked because you were good versus because you were lucky.
Assign every improvement an owner and a date - an action without an owner is a wish.
File the notes where the next crew can find them - the loop closes when the next shift reads it.
stop_conditions: Stop if the after-action becomes a blame session - redirect to process or end it; blame kills every future debrief.
Stop if the review uncovers a safety or legal violation - report it up through proper channels, do not bury it in debrief notes.
Stop if leadership punishes honesty from a prior debrief - escalate; a punished debrief program is worse than none.
Never skip the after-action after the bad shifts - those are the ones with the most to teach.

title: Step Up From Crew Member to Crew Lead
mechanism_check: The lead's mechanism is different from the worker's: the worker produces output; the lead produces output through others.
Promotion to lead fails when the best technician keeps doing technician work - the mechanism requires letting go of the tools to run the crew.
The lead's real product is a crew that functions when the lead is not there.
improvised_tools: A daily plan written before the shift: who does what, in what order, with what - the lead's core tool.
The shift huddle: the lead's daily mechanism for alignment.
A delegation ladder: show, do together, supervise, trust - matched to each crew member's level.
Your mentor's phone number: every new lead needs a lead to call.
steps: Learn the planning before the promotion: volunteer to draft the daily plan while still on the crew.
Shift from doing to assigning: your hands are now the crew's bottleneck if they are on the tools.
Know each crew member's level and assign accordingly - the delegation ladder is per person, not per crew.
Own the problems upward: shield the crew from noise, bring them clear direction.
Evaluate fairly and document continuously - the ledger habit now applies to your people.
Build your replacement: a lead with no successor is a single point of failure.
stop_conditions: Stop doing the crew's work for them to 'save time' - it teaches dependence and hides capacity problems.
Stop if you are asked to lead without the authority to match - responsibility without authority is a trap; clarify it.
Stop playing favorites in assignments or evaluations - perceived unfairness destroys a crew faster than bad planning.
Stop and ask for help when you are drowning - new leads who hide overload fail loudly later.

title: Teach Your Trade to Non-Technical Staff
mechanism_check: Non-technical staff - admin, council aides, the public - need the mechanism, not the trade: why it matters, what it costs, what happens if it is skipped.
The mechanism of good translation: one analogy, one number, one story - the technical detail is the enemy.
When decision-makers understand the mechanism, budgets and priorities follow.
improvised_tools: One strong analogy per concept: the water system as the city's bloodstream, the budget as the fuel gauge.
One honest number per point: what it costs, what failure costs - numbers persuade where jargon does not.
Photos and field visits: ten minutes at the actual pump station beats an hour of slides.
Plain language: if a sentence needs a glossary, rewrite the sentence.
steps: Find out what decision the audience actually faces - teach to the decision, not the topic.
Open with why it matters to them: their street, their water, their budget line.
Explain the mechanism in one analogy, then the one number that proves it.
Show, do not tell: photos, samples, a field visit - tangible beats abstract.
Invite the hard questions and answer them straight - the question they will not ask is the misunderstanding that kills the budget.
Close with the ask: what you need from them, stated plainly.
stop_conditions: Stop if you are being asked to simplify past honesty - 'just tell them it is fine' when it is not is a lie with slides.
Stop if the audience wants a technical rubber stamp for a decision already made - name what you are actually being asked to bless.
Stop using jargon to dodge a hard question - say 'I do not know, I will find out' instead.
Never let a presentation become the decision: your job is informing the deciders, not replacing their judgment.

title: Write a Job-Reclassification Request That Wins
mechanism_check: Reclassification is a job-content mechanism: the request wins when the documented duties provably exceed the current classification.
HR does not reclassify effort or tenure - it reclassifies duties, scope, and required skill. The mechanism is evidence of changed work.
The request is a legal document in a personnel system: precise, factual, and boring is persuasive.
improvised_tools: Your skills ledger: the raw evidence of what you actually do.
The official job description for your current class and the target class - the gap is your argument.
Comparable classifications in neighboring jurisdictions - the market-rate evidence.
Your supervisor's support in writing - a reclassification without it is an uphill fight.
steps: Document your actual duties for 30 to 90 days: what you do, at what level of independence, with what consequences of error.
Map each duty against your current classification's description - highlight everything above it.
Map the same duties against the target classification - show the fit is real, not aspirational.
Gather the comparables: same work, higher class, neighboring agencies.
Write the request as a gap analysis: current class says X, I do Y, target class says Y - with evidence attached.
Submit through your supervisor with their written support; follow the jurisdiction's process exactly.
stop_conditions: Stop if the 'new duties' are actually just more of the same level - volume is not reclassification; scope and complexity are.
Stop inflating duties - HR verifies, and exaggeration discredits the real gap.
Stop if the process requires going around your supervisor - follow the chain; end-runs poison the request.
Never threaten or time the request as leverage in a dispute - it becomes a grievance, not a reclassification.

title: Write SOPs People Actually Follow
mechanism_check: An SOP fails when it is written for the auditor instead of the worker: the mechanism that works is a procedure written for the person doing the job, at the moment of doing it.
The mechanism of a followed SOP: short, sequential, checkable - each step verifiable before moving on.
SOPs that live in binders die in binders; SOPs that live at the work site get used.
improvised_tools: The worker who does the job best: write with them, not about them.
Photos of each critical step - a picture of 'right' beats a paragraph describing it.
A one-page quick reference at the work site; the full SOP in the file.
A trial run: have someone follow the draft cold and note every confusion.
steps: Watch the job done right, step by step, and write down what actually happens - not what the old SOP says.
Write in imperative voice, one action per step, in the order it is performed.
Add the checks: after which steps does the worker verify before continuing.
Include the stop conditions: when to halt and call whom - the SOP's most important section.
Trial it with a competent worker who has not seen the draft - fix every snag they hit.
Review annually or after any incident: SOPs rot as equipment and crews change.
stop_conditions: Stop if the SOP would document a workaround for a broken process - fix the process or escalate; do not canonize the workaround.
Stop if the procedure requires violating a regulation or safety rule - the SOP must never ask that.
Stop writing SOPs nobody will read because the real process is tribal knowledge - get the knowledge first, then write.
Never copy another jurisdiction's SOP verbatim - adapt it to your equipment, your crew, your rules.

title: Run a Shift Huddle That Ends on Time
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: a crew starts the shift with different information, different assumptions, and no shared plan.
The huddle's mechanism is synchronization: same facts, same priorities, same assignments - in the shortest time that achieves it.
A huddle that rambles teaches the crew to tune out; a huddle that ends on time teaches them to show up.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard or paper with three columns: today, who is on what, watch-outs - the huddle's whole agenda.
A timer, visible: time discipline is the huddle's credibility.
The 'parking lot': anything needing more than thirty seconds goes there, not in the huddle.
A rotating facilitator: shared ownership keeps it from becoming one person's lecture.
steps: Start at the same time, same place, every shift - the ritual is the mechanism.
State today's work in priority order: what must get done, in what sequence.
Assign names to tasks - unassigned work is unowned work.
Name the watch-outs: hazards, public events, equipment issues, weather.
Take questions, park the long ones, end on time - every time.
Post the board where the crew can see it all shift - the huddle's output outlives the huddle.
stop_conditions: Stop the huddle from becoming a grievance session - park it, address it separately, protect the ritual.
Stop if the huddle consistently runs long - cut the agenda, not the discipline; investigate what is bloating it.
Stop holding the huddle if leadership never acts on what it surfaces - an ignored huddle is worse than none; escalate the pattern.
Never skip the huddle on the 'easy' days - the ritual's value is in the hard days, and it only exists if it is every day.

title: Hand Off a Live Job Between Crews
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: a job in progress carries invisible state - what is done, what is half-done, what is dangerous - and shift change is where that state gets lost.
The handoff's mechanism is state transfer: the incoming crew must inherit the full picture, not rediscover it.
Most handoff failures are not communication failures - they are assumption failures: 'they must know.'
improvised_tools: A handoff sheet: job, status, what is done, what is next, hazards, open issues - filled before the incoming crew arrives.
Photos of the current state: the half-finished trench, the open panel, the staged materials.
A five-minute overlap: face-to-face beats every written system for the ambiguous parts.
The work order or job file: the handoff writes into the record, not just into memory.
steps: Fill the handoff sheet before shift end: status, next steps, hazards, open issues, materials staged.
Photograph the site's current state - the incoming crew sees what you see.
Walk the incoming lead through it face-to-face: point at the work, not at the paper.
Name the hazards explicitly: what is energized, what is open, what is unstable.
Confirm understanding: have the incoming lead restate the next steps back.
Log the handoff: who gave it, who took it, when - the record closes the loop.
stop_conditions: Stop the handoff if the incoming crew is not qualified for the remaining work - a job handed to the wrong crew is an incident waiting.
Stop if the site cannot be left in a safe state - stay until it is safe or escalate; never hand off a hazard.
Stop if key information is missing and the outgoing crew has left - investigate before proceeding, do not guess.
Never hand off verbally only on a complex or hazardous job - write it down; memory does not survive shift change.

title: Improvise Roles When Half the Crew Is Out
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: the roster you planned for is not the roster you have, but the work and the hazards do not shrink.
The mechanism is capability mapping, not title mapping: who can actually do what safely, regardless of what is on their badge.
The failure mode is role-creep: everyone stretches a little, nobody owns the critical tasks, and the safety net develops holes.
improvised_tools: A capability matrix: names down the side, critical tasks across the top, who is qualified for each - kept current.
The buddy system: pair the stretched with the solid on every critical task.
A stripped priority list: with half a crew, half the work waits - name what waits.
The supervisor's authority to call mutual aid or contractors before the gap becomes a hazard.
steps: Map who is actually here against the day's critical tasks - capability, not title.
Cut the work list to what the present crew can do safely - defer the rest explicitly.
Pair up: nobody works a critical or hazardous task alone on a short crew.
Reassign the safety roles first - spotter, attendant, flagger - before the production roles.
Brief the crew on the changed plan: what is deferred, who is covering what, the new limits.
Call for help early: mutual aid, contractors, or the next shift - short crews that tough it out get hurt.
stop_conditions: Stop any task the present crew is not qualified to do - short staffing never authorizes unqualified work.
Stop if cutting the list still leaves critical safety coverage unfilled - stand down and escalate.
Stop the 'hero shift' mentality: fatigue on a short crew compounds - rotate, rest, or stop.
Stop if the deferrals include life-safety maintenance - escalate in writing; some work cannot wait for full staffing.

title: Coordinate Two Departments on One Work Site
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: two departments, two chains of command, two sets of priorities, one patch of ground.
The mechanism that works is a single site plan with named owners: who does what, in what order, who decides when it changes.
The classic failure is sequence collision: both crews need the same space, the same shutdown, the same morning.
improvised_tools: A one-page site plan: sequence, owners, shared resources, decision authority - signed by both leads.
A daily coordination check: five minutes, both leads, before work starts.
Shared resources scheduled in writing: the shutdown window, the crane time, the road closure.
A single point of contact per department - no cross-crew freelancing.
steps: Meet before mobilization: walk the site together, agree the sequence, name the owners.
Write the one-page plan: who, what order, shared resources, who decides changes.
Schedule the shared constraints first: shutdowns, closures, lifts - the scarcest resources set the schedule.
Hold the daily five-minute check: yesterday's progress, today's plan, conflicts surfacing.
Route all changes through the two leads - no crew-to-crew re-planning on the fly.
Close out together: joint walkthrough, punch list with owners, shared sign-off.
stop_conditions: Stop if the departments' safety rules conflict - apply the stricter one; never split the difference on safety.
Stop work if the sequence breaks down and crews are improvising around each other - re-plan before someone gets hurt.
Stop if one department starts directing the other's crew - chains of command do not merge; coordinate, do not commandeer.
Stop and escalate if the shared resource (shutdown, closure) is being double-booked - the schedule conflict is a leadership problem.

title: Run a Mutual-Aid Request Up the Chain
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: you need help you do not have, from an agency that owes you nothing, through a chain that moves slowly.
The mechanism is pre-built relationships and pre-signed agreements: mutual aid works in the emergency because it was built in the calm.
The request's mechanism: specific need, specific capability, specific duration - vague requests get vague responses.
improvised_tools: Existing mutual-aid agreements, printed and known - the legal foundation of the request.
A resource-typing list: what you need described by capability, not by agency ('one vactor truck with operator,' not 'help').
A single request channel: all requests through one point, so nothing duplicates or contradicts.
A reception plan: where incoming resources report, who briefs them, how they are tracked.
steps: Define the need precisely: capability, quantity, duration, location - the request is a spec, not a plea.
Route it through your chain: the request carries your chief's authority, not just your need.
Send it through the designated channel - the agreement names the channel; use it.
Prepare the reception: staging area, briefing packet, tracking system for incoming resources.
Brief incoming resources on your incident action plan, safety, and communications - they are under your command now.
Demobilize and document: what came, what it cost, thank-yous in writing - the relationship is the real asset.
stop_conditions: Stop if there is no agreement covering the request - document the emergency need and get executive authorization; do not freelance across jurisdictions.
Stop accepting resources you cannot supervise, house, or use - unassigned mutual aid is a liability.
Stop if the incoming resources operate outside your incident action plan - integrate or release.
Stop and track costs from the first hour - mutual aid is reimbursable and auditable; undocumented aid becomes a budget fight.

title: Train as a Team on a Live Exercise
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: training that does not feel real teaches responses that do not work when it is real.
The mechanism of a good exercise: a realistic scenario, real roles, real decisions - with a safety net that the real thing lacks.
The exercise's real product is not the reps - it is the discovery of what breaks before it matters.
improvised_tools: A scenario built from your jurisdiction's actual risks: the flood plain, the hazmat route, the aging infrastructure.
Evaluators with checklists: observers who watch the mechanism, not the theater.
A safety officer with absolute stop authority - the exercise's non-negotiable role.
The after-action template ready before the exercise starts - the learning is the deliverable.
steps: Design the scenario from a real risk: what would actually fail here, and what would the team have to do.
Assign real roles: the people who would do it for real do it in the exercise.
Brief the safety boundaries first: what is simulated, what is real, who can stop the exercise.
Run it: let the team make real decisions, including wrong ones - the mistakes are the curriculum.
Hot-wash immediately: what worked, what broke, while it is fresh.
Write the after-action with owners and dates - an exercise without fixes is theater.
stop_conditions: Stop the exercise the moment anyone's safety is actually at risk - the safety officer's call is final, no debate.
Stop if the exercise is scripting success - a drill that cannot fail teaches nothing.
Stop if participants are being set up to fail publicly for entertainment - the exercise builds the team or it harms it.
Never exercise with live hazards (real fire, real chemicals, real traffic) without the full safety plan of a real incident.

title: Resolve an Interagency Jurisdiction Overlap
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: two agencies both claim it - or neither will - and the work sits in the gap while the public waits.
The mechanism is authority mapping: whose statute, whose asset, whose budget - overlap resolves when the legal facts are on the table.
Most overlaps are not legal disputes; they are communication failures wearing legal costumes.
improvised_tools: The actual statutes, charters, and interlocal agreements - read them, do not rely on lore.
A jurisdiction map: assets and boundaries drawn, not assumed.
A written memorandum of understanding template - the tool that prevents the next overlap.
A neutral facilitator for the hard ones: sometimes the mechanism needs a third chair.
steps: Define the exact overlap: which asset, which service, which decision - vague disputes do not resolve.
Pull the legal facts: statutes, agreements, asset records - what does the paper actually say.
Meet agency to agency at the working level first - most overlaps die at a table with the documents.
Draft the division: who does what, who pays, who decides - specific enough to operate from.
Write it as an MOU and get signatures - memory fades, paper holds.
Build the review date in: jurisdictions change, and the MOU should age gracefully.
stop_conditions: Stop if the overlap involves an active emergency - act first under emergency authority, resolve the paperwork after.
Stop if either side is asserting authority it cannot cite - 'we have always done it' is not a statute.
Stop and get legal counsel involved when the dispute affects liability, regulated assets, or public funds.
Never let the dispute become the public's problem - interim service continues while agencies argue.

title: Improvise a Field Command Post With No Gear
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: an incident needs command, but the command vehicle, the radios, and the plans are somewhere else.
The mechanism of a command post is not the equipment - it is four functions: command, information, communications, and a visible location everyone can find.
A command post fails when it is invisible: if incoming resources cannot find command, there is no command.
improvised_tools: Any vehicle with flashers as the marker - the command post's flag.
A folding table, a whiteboard, paper maps: the information function needs a surface, not a server.
Cell phones as the comms net until radios arrive: a group call is a command net.
Vests or hats marking command staff - visible authority prevents freelancing.
steps: Pick the location: safe, accessible, visible, upwind and uphill of hazards - announce it on every channel you have.
Mark it: vehicle flashers, a sign, a flag - incoming resources must see it before they need it.
Set up the four functions: a command spot, an information board, a comms point, a staging direction.
Start the incident log immediately: time, decisions, resources - the record starts at minute one.
Establish the comms rhythm: check-ins on a schedule, briefings on a cycle.
Transition deliberately when the real gear arrives: transfer the log and the picture, do not restart.
stop_conditions: Stop if the chosen location becomes unsafe - move command; a command post in the hot zone commands nothing.
Stop if command is being bypassed - freelancing units get one redirect, then stand down.
Stop expanding the improvised post past its capability - know when to call for the real mobile command.
Never run command from inside a vehicle with the windows up and the radio off - presence is the mechanism.

title: Hold Standards and Morale Through a Budget Freeze
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: the money stopped, the work did not, and the crew is watching leadership for what the freeze really means.
The mechanism is honest prioritization plus visible fairness: the crew accepts hard constraints they understand and share.
Morale's mechanism is not pep talks - it is competence, fairness, and being told the truth.
improvised_tools: A public priority list: what continues, what pauses, why - posted where the crew sees it.
The recognition that costs nothing: specific praise, in front of peers, for real work.
Cross-training and skill projects: the freeze's downtime is the crew's growth time.
Transparent numbers: show the crew the actual budget picture - adults handle truth better than rumor.
steps: Tell the truth early: what is frozen, for how long, what it means for the crew - rumor fills silence.
Publish the priority list: safety and critical services continue; everything else is ranked openly.
Protect the crew's essentials: safety gear, required training, the tools that keep them safe - freeze the rest first.
Redirect idle capacity to deferred value: training, maintenance, documentation, cross-training.
Recognize relentlessly: name the good work specifically and publicly.
Plan the restart: when the freeze lifts, the crew with a plan recovers fastest.
stop_conditions: Stop if the freeze is being used to cut safety spending - escalate in writing; a freeze never overrides a known hazard.
Stop if 'doing more with less' becomes doing unsafe work with fewer people - name it and stand down the unsafe part.
Stop the rumor mill by communicating on a schedule - silence is a decision, and it is the wrong one.
Stop if the freeze starts driving your best people out - retention of critical skills is a leadership emergency; escalate.

title: Stand Down When the Call Exceeds Your Authority
mechanism_check: The coordination challenge: the situation demands action, the crew wants to act, but the authority, qualification, or legal cover is not yours.
The mechanism is disciplined restraint: knowing the line, holding it under pressure, and handing off cleanly.
Standing down is not quitting - it is the mechanism that keeps an overreach from becoming a liability, an injury, or a crime.
improvised_tools: Your jurisdiction's delegation and authority documents - know your lines before the pressure.
A clear escalation path: who to call, in what order, with what information.
The words to hold the line: state what is outside authority, who can authorize it, and what you can do meanwhile.
A log of the decision: what was asked, why you stood down, who you escalated to.
steps: Recognize the line: authority, qualification, legal cover - name which one is missing.
Hold the crew: brief them on what you can do and what you cannot - ambiguity is what pulls crews across lines.
Do everything inside your authority meanwhile: secure, document, communicate, prepare.
Escalate cleanly: the facts, what is needed, who can authorize it - one clear request up the chain.
Hand off to the authorized party with a full brief - your restraint bought them a clean scene.
Log it: the request, the line, the escalation - the record protects everyone.
stop_conditions: Stop means stop: once you have stood down on authority grounds, do not drift back in 'just to help' - that is how liability attaches.
Stop if anyone - including a superior - orders you to cross a legal line: unlawful orders get refused and documented.
Stop if the pressure is political rather than operational - politics does not grant authority; document the pressure.
Never confuse standing down with abandoning: secure the scene, keep communicating, and stay available to the authorized party.
